common_name: Alba Grandiflora Lotus (Classic Single White Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally, eye pointed outward, in heavy clay soil in a wide, undrained container submerged a few inches below the water surface once water has warmed well past last frost.

directions: Alba Grandiflora is one of the oldest and most widely grown lotus cultivars, prized for its enormous single white blooms that can reach 8 to 10 inches across atop tall stems held well above the round, waxy blue-green leaves. It is a large, vigorous grower best suited to an in-ground pond or a half-barrel-sized container rather than a small tub, since its rhizomes spread quickly in warm weather. Flowers open fragrant over three to four mornings before dropping their petals to reveal the distinctive flat seed pod. Cut back fading leaves and spent pods through the season and divide the tuber bank every two to three years in early spring before growth resumes, discarding old woody sections and replanting only firm, plump tuber tips.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Marliacea Albida Water Lily (Classic Hardy White Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay/loam soil in a wide, shallow container topped with pea gravel, and lower into the pond so the crown sits 12-18 inches below the water surface once water has warmed in spring.

directions: Introduced by the French breeder Latour-Marliac in the 1880s, Marliacea Albida is one of the classic hardy white water lilies still widely grown today, producing star-shaped, faintly fragrant white blooms with golden stamens set against olive-green pads that are often bronze-tinted when young. It is a vigorous, free-flowering grower well suited to medium to large ponds where it can spread across several feet of water surface. Remove yellowing pads and spent flowers regularly to keep the crown tidy and encourage continuous bloom from late spring through early fall. Lift and divide the rhizome every three to four years in spring once the container becomes root-bound, replanting only the youngest, most vigorous rhizome sections.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Blue Beauty Water Lily (Fragrant Tropical Day-Blooming Blue)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond only after water has warmed well above 70F, since tropical water lilies are cold-sensitive.

directions: Blue Beauty is a long-cultivated tropical day-blooming water lily valued for its large, star-shaped, deep violet-blue flowers held several inches above the water on sturdy stems, along with a strong sweet fragrance that carries across a patio pond. Its mottled, purple-flecked pads and free-flowering habit make it a standout centerpiece even in a modest-sized water feature. Because it is a tender tropical, gardeners outside its hardy range typically grow it as a warm-season annual or lift and overwinter the tuber indoors in moist sand once water temperatures drop in fall. Feed monthly with aquatic plant tablets through the growing season and remove spent flowers and yellowing pads to keep the crown vigorous.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Red Flare Water Lily (Tropical Night-Blooming Red)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond once the water has warmed well above 70F; site where evening blooms can be enjoyed after dusk.

directions: Red Flare is a striking tropical night-blooming water lily with deep garnet-red, star-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and stay open into the next morning, paired with distinctive reddish-bronze new foliage that matures to deep purple-green. It is a vigorous grower best suited to a pond large enough to give its spreading pads room, and its evening display makes it a favorite for gardens used mainly after work or entertaining after dark. Because it is a true tropical, it needs consistently warm water and will not survive freezing temperatures, so gardeners north of its hardy range grow it as a seasonal annual or overwinter the dormant tuber indoors in damp sand. Feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets and deadhead spent blooms to keep new flowers coming through summer.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in containers of heavy clay soil and submerge in 4-12 inches of water once water temperatures reach 60F, or plant directly into shallow pond margins.

directions: White pickerelweed is a white-flowered selection of the native marginal aquatic pickerel rush, carrying the same glossy, heart-shaped leaves but producing crisp white flower spikes instead of the species' typical blue-violet, giving a brighter accent among pond-edge plantings. It blooms from early summer into fall and is just as attractive to pollinators, particularly bumblebees and long-tongued bees working the tubular flowers. Plant in shallow standing water in full sun for the strongest flowering and cut back spent spikes to prolong bloom. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, replanting only vigorous rhizome sections with healthy roots attached.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Dwarf Sagittaria (Awl-Leaf Arrowhead, Narrow-Leaf Marginal Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or runners in mucky soil in very shallow water (up to 4 inches deep) or fully submerged as a marginal groundcover once water has warmed in spring.

directions: Unlike its larger, arrow-leaved cousins, dwarf sagittaria forms low, grassy tufts of narrow ribbon-like leaves that spread by runners to knit together a dense groundcover along the shallow edges of a pond, making it useful for softening liner edges and stabilizing muddy margins. Small white three-petaled flowers appear on short stalks above the foliage in summer, though the plant is grown mainly for its neat, low texture rather than for bloom. It tolerates both shallow standing water and fully submerged conditions, and is also widely sold for planted aquariums. Thin congested patches periodically by pulling and replanting runners, since it can spread quickly in nutrient-rich water.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Variegated Yellow Flag Iris (Striped-Leaf Water Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet, fertile soil in shallow standing water up to 6 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Variegated yellow flag iris carries the same bright yellow spring flowers and bold sword-shaped foliage as the species, but its leaves emerge crisply striped in cream and green, gradually fading to solid green as summer heats up. The strong upright form and eye-catching spring foliage make it a striking accent at a pond margin or bog garden, especially paired against darker-leaved marginals. Because straight-species yellow flag iris is classified as invasive in parts of North America and Australia, gardeners in those regions should confirm local guidance before planting even variegated selections and should avoid siting it near natural waterways. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or right after flowering to maintain both vigor and the strength of the variegation.

common_name: Colchesteri Japanese Water Iris (Marbled Blue-and-White Rabbit-Ear Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet, fertile soil in shallow standing water up to 4 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Colchesteri is an old, widely grown Japanese water iris cultivar prized for its distinctive white flowers heavily marbled and veined in violet-blue, giving each bloom a mottled, painterly look quite different from the solid blue-purple flowers of the species. Like other rabbit-ear irises, it tolerates standing water far better than bearded types, making it a reliable structural accent for the shallow-water zone of a pond alongside pickerelweed and arrowhead. It flowers in late spring to early summer above narrow, upright sword-shaped foliage that stays tidy through the season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or immediately after flowering to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Minimus Aureus Dwarf Golden Sweet Flag (Miniature Gold-Striped Grassy Marginal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich soil at the pond margin or in shallow water up to 1 inch deep, or grow in a container as a small-scale accent.

directions: Minimus Aureus is the smallest commonly grown sweet flag cultivar, forming tight, tufted rosettes of narrow gold-and-green striped grassy foliage that stay only a few inches tall, making it well suited to the front edge of a pond margin, a rock crevice, or a small container water garden where larger marginals would overwhelm the scale. Its dense, slow-spreading habit works well tucked between stepping stones at a bog edge or massed as a low, colorful groundcover. It prefers consistently moist to wet soil and tolerates very shallow standing water but does not need to be submerged to thrive. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to refresh vigor and control spread.

common_name: Variegated Sweet Flag (Striped Calamus, Fragrant Marginal Grass-Like Perennial)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in wet, fertile soil at the pond margin or in shallow water up to 4 inches deep in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Variegated sweet flag is a much larger, bolder plant than the dwarf gramineus cultivars, sending up broad, iris-like fans of cream-and-green striped leaves that release a sweet, spicy fragrance when bruised or crushed, an old trait that gave the species its common name and long history of use in herbal sachets. Its upright, strap-like foliage provides strong vertical texture and brightness at a pond edge or bog garden, contrasting well with rounded-leaf marginals like pickerelweed. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form a substantial clump over a few seasons but is far less assertive than the invasive-listed straight species can be in some regions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain the crispness of the variegation and control spread.
